name: Fishmans
discourse_profile: Sato directed by atmosphere rather than arrangement — 'Here's the mood I'm going for, let's see what everyone can come up with' — using an outmoded Akai sampler to build demos that established emotional targets for the band to interpret. The governing principle was reduction: producer ZAK, whom Motegi compares to George Martin, 'showed us how to strip things back, and reduce our music to the bare essentials,' teaching that 'when you keep adding sounds, you lose that tension.' Sato's own conviction was uncompromising — 'You don't have to make compromises in your work... If I stop, it's over' — and he had no patience for the media game, remaining a difficult interviewee throughout his career. Their private studio Waikiki Beach was essential: 'The less such things we had, the better Fishmans became,' with liberation from studio-clock pressure allowing Sato to record alone, preserving states that wouldn't survive a commercial session. Motegi describes the band's emotional register as inseparable from duality — 'not only to feel happy but also to maintain the feeling of loneliness' — and frames their music as refusing closure: 'never draw conclusions, nor does it seek conclusions... it's like putting a part of everyday life into music.' The sound evolved from ska and rocksteady through dub and sample-based influence (Arrested Development, Massive Attack, Beck) toward the infinite-loop structures of Long Season — a single 35-minute piece whose five sections Sato described as operating in 'a flow that's different from the ordinary flow of time.' Motegi insists the music is not retrospective: 'If the music felt like a throwback when we played it, I don't think I'd be as interested.'
